paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification predicts a label by taking a vote among nearby labeled examples. Its appeal includes adapting automatically to changes in the scale of the data distribution. Active learning introduces another choice: which examples should receive labels? The challenge is to make that choice intelligently while preserving the local voting behavior that makes nearest-neighbor methods useful.

This paper introduces a two-stage active learning algorithm for training these classifiers. Its distinguishing feature is that predictions still use a vote among the k nearest neighbors. The authors describe it as the first active learning approach in this setting to retain that prediction rule, and establish consistency guarantees for a modified classifier trained on the acquired samples.

The stronger rate result requires specific conditions: sufficiently smooth conditional label probabilities and the Tsybakov noise condition. Under those assumptions, the actively trained classifiers approach the Bayes-optimal classifier faster asymptotically than passively trained nearest-neighbor classifiers. This is a conditional advantage in learning rate, rather than a promise of improvement on every dataset.
icml-2023-a-two-stage-active-learning-al.tldr: A two-stage active learning method preserves nearest-neighbor voting and achieves faster asymptotic convergence under stated smoothness and noise conditions.

paragraphs: Finding formulas for mathematical constants often depends on recognizing a pattern that suggests a useful identity. Automated efforts based on exhaustive search face a different bottleneck: they can examine only a limited space of candidate expressions. This paper proposes searching through patterns in integer sequences representing constants, giving automated discovery a different source of structure to exploit.

The proposed ESMA algorithm builds on the Berlekamp–Massey algorithm to identify those patterns. Its search produces both previously known formulas and new conjectures involving e, e squared, tan(1), and ratios of Bessel-function values. The distinction between a recovered formula and a new conjecture matters: the latter is a proposed mathematical relationship, rather than a proof supplied merely by finding a pattern.

Many of the resulting expressions converge numerically faster than the corresponding simple continued fractions. The authors also characterize which constants the method can capture and quantify its algorithmic advantage in certain scenarios. Together, these results support sequence analysis as a way to assist mathematical intuition and generate promising relationships for further investigation.
icml-2023-automated-search-for-conjectur.tldr: ESMA searches integer-sequence patterns to recover known formulas and propose new conjectures for mathematical constants.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks depend strongly on how parts of an input combine into a larger structure. Recursive neural networks address this by composing representations recursively, but learning the underlying structure introduces choices about which compositions to pursue. Beam Tree Recursive Cell, or BT-Cell, adds beam search to this process so that the model can consider multiple candidate latent structures.

The framework is designed to work with backpropagation. The authors also introduce a relaxation of the hard top-k selections used in beam search, aiming to let gradient signals propagate more effectively through those decisions. This connects a search procedure for choosing structures with the continuous optimization used to train neural networks.

Across out-of-distribution evaluations, BT-Cell achieves nearly perfect results on several demanding synthetic tasks, including ListOps and logical inference, while matching the performance of other recursive models on realistic data. The study also uncovers a failure when neural models face unseen numbers of arguments in ListOps. That finding distinguishes success on some structural tests from reliable generalization across all structural changes.
icml-2023-beam-tree-recursive-cells-35e0.tldr: BT-Cell makes beam search compatible with training recursive networks, achieving strong structural-task results while exposing a specific generalization failure.

paragraphs: A certified neural-network watermark comes with a mathematical guarantee against a defined class of removal attacks. Earlier work used randomized smoothing to obtain guarantees for attacks bounded in the l2 norm. The difficulty is that this approach can fail to give meaningful certificates in high-dimensional parameter spaces when attacks are measured using lp norms with p greater than two.

This paper replaces that smoothing approach with one based on mollifier theory. For the proposed smooth classifier, the authors obtain a certified radius that does not depend on parameter dimension. Their formulation covers lp-norm watermark removal attacks throughout the range from p equal to one through infinity, extending the range of attack measurements addressed by the certificate.

The paper also develops an approximation using partial differential equation theory. Its purpose is to ease the sampling and prediction costs associated with randomized smoothing and the numerical integration costs of mollifier smoothing, while retaining the watermark certification. The contribution therefore joins a broader dimensional robustness guarantee with a method intended to make the required smoothing computation more practical.
icml-2023-dimension-independent-certifie.tldr: Mollifier smoothing provides dimension-independent watermark certificates across lp attack norms, with a PDE-based approximation to reduce computational difficulty.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization works from function evaluations rather than directly available derivatives. This is useful in problems where an algorithm can measure an outcome but cannot obtain a gradient. In nonconvex problems, however, it must also handle saddle points: places where progress can appear to stall even though directions of improvement remain.

Previous results showed efficient saddle escape for methods using a number of evaluations per iteration proportional to the dimension. This paper asks whether estimators built from just two evaluations can also escape. The authors show that adding an appropriate isotropic perturbation at every iteration enables an algorithm using 2m evaluations, for any m between one and the dimension, to find approximate second-order stationary points in polynomial time.

The stated total evaluation bound scales, up to suppressed logarithmic factors, as d divided by m times epsilon squared times a parameter measuring strict-saddle structure. That parameter is itself bounded below at approximately the square root of epsilon. The result establishes that very small per-iteration evaluation budgets can support saddle escape; it does not claim to find a global optimum.
icml-2023-escaping-saddle-points-in-zero.tldr: With suitable isotropic perturbations, even two-point zeroth-order estimators can efficiently reach approximate second-order stationary points.

paragraphs: Neural Collapse describes a pattern in trained classifiers: representations of examples from the same class gather around their class mean, and the final layer's weights align with those representations. This paper investigates whether related organization appears inside the network, rather than only at its final feature layer. The focus is an empirical account of how representations change across depth.

The authors track representation means and covariances at different layers. They find that variation among examples from the same class becomes smaller relative to variation between classes as one moves deeper into a trained network. This describes increasing class separation in relative terms; it does not require interpreting every layer as eliminating all variation within a class.

In upper layers where between-class variation dominates, the space defined by class means also aligns with the leading singular-vector directions of the corresponding weight matrix. This connects the geometry of learned features to the dominant directions of the layer's weights. The paper additionally discusses a relationship with associative memories, placing these observed patterns alongside another perspective on storing and organizing information.
icml-2023-feature-learning-in-deep-class.tldr: An empirical study finds increasingly class-organized representations across network depth and alignment between upper-layer class means and dominant weight directions.

paragraphs: Predicting from noisy multivariate time series requires useful summaries of several quantities evolving together. This paper introduces programmable feature engineering: a framework that automatically generates many predictive features while allowing users to express their own inductive biases with little effort. The aim is to combine large-scale feature generation with a manageable way to influence what the features represent.

The framework starts from a fine-grained view of a time series as an accumulated sequence of small trajectory increments. Each increment is governed by a proposed spin-gas dynamical Ising model. This modeling perspective motivates a compact collection of operators that summarize multivariate trajectories at an abstract level, forming the building blocks of the feature-generation system.

The significance of those operators is that a small vocabulary can support many derived features, rather than requiring every summary to be designed separately. The authors numerically evaluate the method on several synthetic and real-world noisy time-series datasets and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is a programmable framework for constructing predictive representations, with empirical support across those evaluated settings.
icml-2023-feature-programming-for-multiv.tldr: A programmable feature-engineering framework uses a fine-grained dynamical view of time series to generate predictive summaries guided by user assumptions.

paragraphs: Regularization helps neural networks generalize by expressing preferences during training. Standard methods usually act on model parameters, which makes it difficult to state directly how predictions should behave. This paper develops a probabilistic route to regularizing predictive functions, allowing desired behavior to enter training more explicitly than through parameter preferences alone.

The authors interpret parameter regularization as specifying an empirical prior over model parameters. From that starting point, they derive function-space empirical Bayes, or FS-EB. The method combines parameter-space and function-space regularization, so preferences can address both the model's numerical representation and the functions it produces. They describe the resulting approach as mathematically simple, straightforward to implement, and requiring little additional computation.

Empirical evaluations report nearly perfect semantic-shift detection, well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, successful adaptation of pretrained models to tasks, and better generalization under covariate shift. These findings show several ways that explicit preferences about predictive behavior can be useful. Their scope is the evaluated settings: the reported outcomes support the method's utility without establishing that every possible functional preference will improve every application.
icml-2023-function-space-regularization-.tldr: FS-EB combines parameter and function regularization to encode desired predictive behavior, with empirical benefits for uncertainty, adaptation, and distribution shifts.

paragraphs: A model trained to satisfy fairness goals can behave differently when deployed on data with changed relationships between labels and sensitive groups. This paper studies such changes as correlation shifts. The issue is more specific than a general change in the data distribution: the label-group association that shaped training may no longer match the association encountered in deployment.

The authors analytically identify limits on accuracy and group fairness for existing methods that enforce fairness during training. They then add a preprocessing step that samples the input data to address the correlation shift. An optimization problem determines how to adjust the proportions of examples across labels and sensitive groups so that the processed data reflects the shifted correlation.

The approach assigns different jobs to the two stages: preprocessing adjusts correlations, while the existing training procedure mitigates unfairness on the adjusted data. This makes the proposal a way to improve those training methods. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report gains in both accuracy and fairness, supporting the value of explicitly addressing label-group shifts before applying fairness-aware training.
icml-2023-improving-fair-training-under-.tldr: Optimizing label-group sampling proportions before fairness-aware training improves accuracy and fairness under the correlation shifts studied.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using the current context and learn from the outcomes. With infinitely many possible actions, a useful approach combines smoothed regret guarantees with reduction to regression, keeping computation independent of action-set size. The paper identifies a practical problem with the resulting interaction data: it lacks well-defined importance weights needed by downstream analyses such as offline model selection.

The proposed online algorithm preserves an equivalent smoothed regret guarantee while generating data with well-defined importance weights. The contribution therefore concerns both the quality of online decisions and the usability of the records those decisions produce. It makes data reuse part of the algorithm's design, rather than treating logged interactions as an automatically adequate resource for later analysis.

This improvement has a computational tradeoff. Online cost increases to an order governed by smoothness, but remains independent of the action set. The result removes a specific obstacle to using smoothed-regret methods in production: obtaining strong online guarantees need not leave subsequent offline model-selection processes without the importance weights they require.
icml-2023-infinite-action-contextual-ban.tldr: An infinite-action contextual bandit algorithm preserves smoothed regret guarantees while producing importance-weighted data usable for downstream analysis.

paragraphs: A learned model of a nonlinear system does not automatically provide the structure needed to design a stabilizing controller. Even when the dynamics are known, constructing feedback that produces stable behavior can be difficult. This paper focuses on learning a particular representation of the dynamics because that representation is directly useful for controller construction.

The controller is a state-dependent nonlinear tracking formulation based on a state-dependent Riccati equation. It applies to nonlinear control-affine systems and relies on a nonlinear factorization of the vector fields describing their dynamics. The authors state that this factorization exists under mild smoothness assumptions, and propose learning it from a finite dataset.

Experiments on several simulated nonlinear systems show that controllers built from the learned factorization can track trajectories stably. The authors also test approaches that jointly learn a controller and a stabilizability certificate for known dynamics, finding them comparatively fragile in their experiments. The broader lesson is supported empirically: learning structure tailored to control can be useful beyond simply fitting a general dynamical model.
icml-2023-learning-control-oriented-dyna.tldr: Learning a control-relevant factorization of nonlinear dynamics enables effective trajectory tracking in simulated systems.

paragraphs: Training on a selected subset can save resources, but choosing that subset may itself require expensive preliminary training. Gradient-based selection methods need sufficiently stable gradient signals; a very short warm-up can leave those signals unreliable. This paper targets that preliminary cost, which can otherwise consume a substantial part of the savings from subset training.

The method distributes lightweight initial training across workers, each using a small, disjoint portion of the data. Data-driven sparsity and augmentation encourage diversity among the locally trained models. Those models are then merged into a centralized model through a model-soup approach used at initialization. The merged model supplies stabilized gradients for selecting the subset on which the main training proceeds.

The design minimizes communication between workers and is evaluated with ResNet and WideResNet models on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. One reported setting, CIFAR-10 with ResNet18, achieves a 15.4-fold preliminary-training speedup and a 2.8-fold overall speedup without accuracy loss. The difference between those gains matters: reducing selection preparation substantially can translate into a smaller, but still meaningful, improvement for the complete training process.
icml-2023-lowering-the-pre-training-tax-.tldr: Lightweight distributed model merging reduces the warm-up cost of gradient-based subset selection, with reported end-to-end training savings.

paragraphs: A sequence model may learn an algorithmic task at one set of lengths yet struggle when sequences become longer. This paper studies whether position-based cross-attention can help a sequence-to-sequence network maintain the right input-output correspondence as length changes. Its focus is the positioning behavior of attention during lookup and copying tasks.

The authors first combine relative attention with interpolation between the original encoded input and its reversed representation. This simple construction produces nearly perfect length generalization on forward and reverse lookup or copy tasks. They then construct harder diagnostic tasks in which the relative distance to the correct attention position changes with the output timestep.

On those harder tasks, interpolation with relative attention is insufficient. The paper introduces new location-attention variants to address that challenge and also reports benefits for length generalization on SCAN and CFQ. The progression of tasks matters: it separates success when positional relationships are easier to maintain from cases requiring the attention mechanism to handle changing relative distances as generation proceeds.
icml-2023-monotonic-location-attention-f.tldr: Position-based attention improves length generalization, with new location-attention variants addressing tasks that defeat a simpler interpolation approach.

paragraphs: In multi-agent best-arm identification, several agents collaborate to determine which available option is best. Communication lets them combine evidence, but their messages can also reveal sensitive information. This paper studies how to preserve the benefit of collaboration while giving formal privacy guarantees for the information exchanged during the search.

The authors consider two privacy definitions: differential privacy and a separate notion called (epsilon, eta)-privacy. These definitions withhold different kinds of information, so the paper develops an algorithm for each rather than treating privacy as one undifferentiated requirement. Both algorithms use a two-level successive-elimination scheme, progressively narrowing the set of candidate arms as the collaborative identification process proceeds.

The theoretical results address privacy, identification accuracy, and sample complexity together. These are the central requirements of the task: protect communication, choose the best arm accurately, and control how much evidence is needed. Experiments in several settings support the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore a formally analyzed way to coordinate private identification, with empirical evidence accompanying the guarantees.
icml-2023-multi-agent-best-arm-identific.tldr: Two successive-elimination algorithms let agents collaboratively identify the best arm with guarantees for privacy, accuracy, and sample complexity.

paragraphs: One explanation for neural-network generalization is that training learns simpler patterns before more complex ones. This paper examines simplicity through the statistics of the input distribution. Its central finding is that networks trained with stochastic gradient descent initially classify using lower-order statistics, such as means and covariances, and only later exploit higher-order statistical structure.

The authors call this pattern distributional simplicity bias. They first demonstrate it in a solvable single-neuron model trained on synthetic data, where the phenomenon can be studied in a controlled mathematical setting. They then examine deep convolutional networks and vision transformers trained on CIFAR-10, and also find the pattern in networks pretrained on ImageNet.

This perspective links the sequence of learned behaviors to the structure present in the data, extending discussion beyond whether a classifier is linear or nonlinear. The evidence spans an analytically tractable example and empirical studies of larger models. The paper also discusses relationships to other simplicity biases and implications for Gaussian universality, connecting the observed training progression to broader questions about which distributional details matter for learning.
icml-2023-neural-networks-trained-with-s.tldr: The study finds that SGD-trained networks use lower-order input statistics early and exploit higher-order structure later in training.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy using a fixed dataset. A common safeguard keeps its actions close to those of the policy that collected the data. The paper argues that constraints based on that policy's distribution or support can be overly restrictive at individual states, especially when the original behavior was suboptimal.

Policy Regularization with Dataset Constraint, or PRDC, instead searches the entire dataset for the nearest state-action sample during a policy update. It uses that sample's action to constrain the learned policy. This allows guidance to come from a suitable example elsewhere in the dataset, including an action that was not recorded together with the particular state being updated.

The softer constraint aims to permit improvement while retaining protection against unsupported actions. The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence that PRDC can reduce value overestimation, with a bounded performance gap. They also report state-of-the-art results on the locomotion and navigation tasks evaluated. These findings support using proximity to dataset examples as a more flexible source of conservatism in offline learning.
icml-2023-policy-regularization-with-dat.tldr: PRDC constrains offline policies using nearby state-action examples from the full dataset, enabling more flexible actions while reducing value overestimation.

paragraphs: People may know useful parts of a reinforcement-learning problem without having a complete world model or a finished policy. RLang provides a language for communicating that partial knowledge to an agent. Its scope covers every element of a Markov decision process, extending beyond languages dedicated to a single component such as rewards or policy behavior.

The paper defines both the syntax of RLang programs and precise semantics for translating their statements into usable information. A parser produces a partial world model and policy that are independent of any particular learning algorithm. That separation matters because the same language can express domain knowledge without tying its meaning to one agent's internal implementation.

The authors demonstrate the language through example programs used by a broad range of reinforcement-learning methods. These include model-based and model-free tabular algorithms, policy-gradient and value-based approaches, hierarchical methods, and deep learning methods. The contribution is a common interface for supplying incomplete knowledge across these settings, with examples showing how different learners can use the resulting information.
icml-2023-rlang-a-declarative-language-f.tldr: RLang translates partial domain knowledge into an algorithm-independent world model and policy that different reinforcement-learning methods can use.

paragraphs: When a Markov decision process has uncertain model parameters, robust planning commonly chooses a policy by optimizing its worst-case return. That can provide reliability with limited data, but the worst-case perspective can also be highly conservative. This paper proposes organizing the decision around a user-specified performance target under model ambiguity.

Robust satisficing MDPs place soft constraints on the expected returns of feasible policies to encourage achievement of that target. The target therefore enters the mathematical formulation directly, rather than being judged only after worst-case optimization. The authors derive a tractable reformulation and develop a first-order optimization method intended to handle large problem instances.

In experiments, the resulting policies achieve targets substantially above the optimal worst-case returns computed by robust MDPs. This comparison does not turn the higher targets into worst-case guarantees; it reflects the different performance criteria used by the two formulations. The authors also report competitive average and percentile performance and demonstrate the algorithm's scalability relative to a state-of-the-art commercial solver.
icml-2023-robust-satisficing-mdps-04f28f.tldr: Robust satisficing MDPs use soft performance targets under model ambiguity, offering a tractable alternative to conservative worst-case planning.

paragraphs: Data poisoning changes training examples to influence a model's predictions. Some certified defenses train multiple base models and combine their predictions by majority vote. This paper argues that such voting leaves useful information unused: a model's output scores contain more than just the identity of its highest-scoring class.

Run-Off Election uses two voting rounds. Base models first vote for their preferred class, and the two leading classes advance to a second election. This gives the ensemble another opportunity to use the base models' preferences when deciding between the finalists. The authors integrate the aggregation rule with Deep Partition Aggregation and Finite Aggregation, producing two modified defenses.

Evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB report certified-accuracy improvements of up to 3–4%. Combining the rule with a boosted version of Deep Partition Aggregation yields reported improvements of roughly 12–27% over the existing state of the art. In many evaluated cases, it also outperforms that reference using 32 times less computation. The results show that aggregation design can materially affect pointwise poisoning certificates.
icml-2023-run-off-election-improved-prov.tldr: A two-round ensemble vote uses more of the base models' output information to improve certified robustness against training-data poisoning.

paragraphs: Random features approximate kernel computations using random projections. This paper asks how coordinating the geometry of those projections can improve approximation accuracy. Simplex Random Features, or SimRFs, correlate projection vectors geometrically while preserving unbiased estimates of the softmax and Gaussian kernels, meaning the estimates remain correct on average.

The authors prove that SimRFs achieve the lowest mean squared error within a specified family: positive random-feature mechanisms with weight-independent geometric coupling. Within that setting, they substantially outperform Orthogonal Random Features without observable additional cost. The scope of the theorem matters because it establishes optimality within this class of mechanisms, rather than among every possible kernel approximation.

A more expensive variant, SimRFs+, allows dependence between vector directions and norms. It is proved asymptotically optimal in that broader family of coupling schemes. Empirical studies report consistent gains in individual kernel estimates, nonparametric classification, and scalable Transformers. Together, the theory and experiments show that carefully arranged randomness can improve approximation quality and benefit downstream uses of the approximated kernels.
icml-2023-simplex-random-features-d1f339.tldr: SimRFs geometrically coordinate random projections to improve unbiased kernel approximation, with optimality guarantees within specified feature families.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption supports computation on encrypted client data, making it attractive for private cloud-based neural-network inference. Its practical obstacle is speed: encrypted operations can be far slower than their plaintext counterparts. SpENCNN addresses inference latency by designing the network's sparsity pattern and the packing of encrypted data together.

The framework first groups convolution channels according to data size and ciphertext size. A group-interleaved encoding then places those groups into the same ciphertext, reducing operations that bottleneck encrypted convolution. It also introduces sub-block weight pruning tailored to homomorphic encryption. Both components target the actual cost of encrypted computation, connecting which weights remain with how the data is represented.

The experiments report overall speedups of 8.37 times for LeNet, 12.11 times for VGG-5, 19.26 times for HEFNet, and 1.87 times for ResNet-20, with negligible accuracy loss. The differing gains show that the measured benefit varies across the evaluated architectures. The central finding is that coordinating packing and sparsity can substantially reduce encrypted inference costs while largely preserving prediction accuracy.
icml-2023-spencnn-orchestrating-encoding.tldr: SpENCNN jointly designs encrypted data packing and model sparsity to accelerate private neural-network inference with negligible reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Self-predictive learning methods such as BYOL and SimSiam learn useful representations without collapsing to trivial outputs. This paper seeks a simple mathematical explanation for that behavior. It starts from the importance of the predictor network and the stop-gradient operation, asking what role these components play in shaping learned representations.

Using linear algebra, the authors show that an optimal linear predictor is close to an orthogonal projection. They build an interpretation around orthonormalization, which organizes representation directions into an orthogonal structure. Within this framework, BYOL's exponential moving average and stop-gradient operation act as an efficient orthonormalization mechanism, providing an explanation of how these training ingredients work together.

The analysis also motivates four predictor variants with closed-form expressions. In ImageNet evaluations after 100 and 300 training epochs, these variants outperform BYOL with a standard trainable linear predictor on top-1 linear accuracy. This links the proposed interpretation to a concrete design change. The explanation specifically develops from the linear-predictor setting, while the experiments support the usefulness of the resulting predictor constructions.
icml-2023-the-edge-of-orthogonality-a-si.tldr: An orthonormalization perspective explains key BYOL components and motivates closed-form predictors that improve the reported ImageNet linear-evaluation results.

paragraphs: Multi-view self-supervised learning learns representations from related views of data, but its different method families are not equally well understood. Contrastive approaches have a familiar connection to mutual information through the InfoNCE bound. This paper develops another perspective using a lower bound composed of entropy and reconstruction terms.

Through this entropy-reconstruction bound, the authors show that clustering-based methods such as DeepCluster and SwAV maximize mutual information. For distillation-based methods such as BYOL and DINO, they identify a more specific division of roles: the methods explicitly maximize reconstruction while implicitly encouraging stable entropy. Empirical results support that interpretation, connecting these methods through a shared analytical framework without assigning them identical mechanisms.

The authors also replace objectives in common multi-view methods with the proposed bound. The resulting training achieves competitive performance and is more stable with smaller batches or smaller exponential-moving-average coefficients. The contribution therefore goes beyond explaining existing objectives: it supplies an alternative objective whose separated terms help account for behavior and whose reported experiments show practical stability benefits.
icml-2023-the-role-of-entropy-and-recons.tldr: An entropy-reconstruction bound connects several self-supervised learning families and provides competitive objectives with improved stability in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation in reinforcement learning asks how much return a given policy is expected to produce. Classical temporal-difference learning focuses directly on this mean return. Quantile temporal-difference learning takes a richer route, learning predictions about the distribution of possible returns. This paper studies whether that additional distributional information can help even when the final quantity of interest is only the mean.

The authors analyze quantile temporal-difference learning for temporal-difference-based policy evaluation. Their conclusion is that learning the return distribution may produce better value estimates than approaches that predict only its mean. The important distinction is between the information represented during learning and the information ultimately requested: a richer prediction target can be useful even when the user wants a single expected value.

The stated benefit can arise in the tabular setting, so it is not presented solely as a consequence of using a complex neural representation. The claim remains a possibility rather than a universal ranking of algorithms. It gives a statistical reason to consider distributional learning for ordinary value estimation, beyond applications that explicitly need the full distribution of outcomes.
icml-2023-the-statistical-benefits-of-qu.tldr: Learning return quantiles may improve mean-value estimation over classical temporal-difference learning, even in tabular policy evaluation.

paragraphs: When a transition model is estimated from sparse or noisy data, planners sometimes lower the discount factor to shorten the effective planning horizon. This is usually understood as reducing the influence of delayed consequences. The paper provides another interpretation that reveals how this regularization interacts with uneven amounts of transition data.

The authors show an optimal-policy equivalence between lowering the discount factor and planning with a transition prior that uses the same distribution across states and actions. Under this interpretation, discount regularization behaves like a prior that regularizes more strongly where more transition data is available. That uneven effect can produce poor performance when some state-action pairs have many observations and others have few.

The equivalence theorem leads to an explicit formula for setting regularization separately for each state-action pair. This replaces a single global adjustment with local choices that address the identified problem. Experiments in simple examples and a medical cancer simulator demonstrate failures of discount regularization and improvements from the proposed remedy. The result makes data coverage central to understanding what a shorter planning horizon actually does.
icml-2023-the-unintended-consequences-of.tldr: A prior-based interpretation exposes problems with global discount regularization and motivates state-action-specific regularization.
